name: Ollama
title: How Ollama Runs Locally: GGUF, CUDA and MLX | Language Lineage
h1: What Actually Runs When You Send Ollama a Prompt?
description: Trace a local Ollama request through its Go service and a supported llama.cpp or MLX engine, separating CPU, NVIDIA CUDA and Apple-silicon Metal execution.
og_subtitle: Local request → Go service → compatible engine → CPU / CUDA / Metal
verified_against: the Ollama API and FAQ, Go server source, GGUF and MLX announcements, llama.cpp build documentation and MLX kernel documentation
scope: Local text inference with downloaded models supported by the selected engine: GGUF/llama.cpp on CPU or NVIDIA CUDA, or the documented MLX engine on Apple silicon. These are version- and model-dependent illustrative paths, not a user-facing engine-switch command or a guarantee of universal model compatibility. Cloud models, AMD/Vulkan routes, partial offload, multimodal processing and detailed token sampling are not depicted.
answer: **Ollama serves requests and selects a compatible model runner; the runner executes numerical work.** Current documented local paths include llama.cpp-backed GGUF support and an MLX engine for supported Apple-silicon models. A Go service does not mean the matrix kernels are Go code, and an Ollama API request does not prove inference is local: cloud endpoints are separate.

sections.heading: Is Ollama itself the model or the inference engine?
paragraphs: Ollama provides request handling, model management and compatible runners. The [Go server source](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/server/routes.go) shows validation and scheduling before inference. The model’s weights are data consumed by an execution engine; neither the model nor the chat endpoint is a programming language.

The diagram distinguishes the service layer from the numerical runtime. This matters when answering what Ollama is written in: Go is evidence for its service implementation, while the selected native engine has its own implementation and kernels. The [llama.cpp path](/ai/how-llama-cpp-runs) and [MLX path](/ai/how-mlx-runs) explain those layers in more detail.

sections.heading: Does every Ollama model use llama.cpp?
paragraphs: No. The [GGUF support announcement](https://ollama.com/blog/improved-performance-and-model-support-with-gguf) documents llama.cpp integration alongside Ollama’s MLX engine. The [MLX announcement](https://ollama.com/blog/mlx) describes an Apple-silicon path for supported architectures. Model compatibility and the installed version determine which claims apply.

The controls compare documented paths; they do not expose a real Ollama engine-selection API. A compatible GGUF route and an MLX route need not accept identical model files or support identical features. Do not infer the engine from a model’s marketing name alone.

sections.heading: Why does Ollama use the CPU instead of the GPU?
paragraphs: A CPU-only model can run in system memory. GPU execution additionally needs a compatible engine, hardware support, dependencies and enough available memory for the configured workload. The [FAQ](https://docs.ollama.com/faq) documents ollama ps and its PROCESSOR column, including fully CPU, fully GPU and mixed placement. That report is more informative than assuming a GPU installation guarantees full offload.

The CUDA choice illustrates supported offloaded work. Real deployments can use a mixture of CPU and GPU, especially when the model does not fit entirely on a device. The diagram excludes that partial-offload detail rather than asserting that all CUDA requests are GPU-only.

sections.heading: What changes on Apple silicon?
paragraphs: The documented MLX engine uses Apple’s array framework and unified-memory architecture for supported models. MLX GPU primitives are implemented using Metal, as the [extension guide](https://ml-explore.github.io/mlx/build/html/dev/extensions.html) explains. This is different from treating a Mac as an NVIDIA CUDA system.

Other local routes can still exist on Macs. The point of the MLX branch is to show one verified engine path, not to claim every model on every Apple computer uses it. Check installed-version release notes and model support before applying this diagram to a specific deployment.

sections.heading: Does using the Ollama API mean my request stays local?
paragraphs: No. The [API introduction](https://docs.ollama.com/api/introduction) documents both local and cloud base URLs, and local servers can also be used with cloud models. This page deliberately chooses a downloaded local model. Endpoint, model selection and serving configuration establish the execution boundary; the client library name alone does not.

sections.heading: How do GGUF, model size and hardware fit together?
paragraphs: GGUF is a model file format consumed by a compatible runtime. It does not describe one fixed processor or make all model architectures interchangeable. Memory placement and the chosen backend determine where computation occurs. This page avoids model rankings, speed promises and guessed internals, and records the engine and device conditions for each illustrated path.

stages.summary: A client sends a chat request to the local Ollama service using an already downloaded supported model.

evidence.quote: For local inference, use http://localhost:11434/api/chat with a downloaded model and omit the authorization header.

stages.name: Ollama Go service
stages.summary: The service handles the request and validates model capabilities and options before selecting a runner.

evidence.quote: scheduleRunner schedules a runner after validating inputs such as capabilities and model options.

stages.name: Runner scheduling
stages.summary: Ollama schedules a compatible engine for the chosen model. This is not a promise that every architecture uses llama.cpp.

evidence.quote: scheduleRunner schedules a runner after validating inputs such as capabilities and model options.

stages.name: llama.cpp GGUF path
stages.summary: The selected compatible GGUF model runs through Ollama’s documented llama.cpp integration.

evidence.quote: GGUF model compatibility through llama.cpp

stages.name: MLX engine
stages.summary: Supported Apple-silicon model paths can use Ollama’s MLX engine, which is distinct from the GGUF/llama.cpp route.

evidence.quote: Ollama on Apple silicon is now built on top of Apple’s machine learning framework, MLX

stages.name: ggml CPU kernels
stages.summary: The selected CPU-only llama.cpp route uses CPU numerical kernels. No universal GPU requirement is implied.

evidence.quote: AVX, AVX2, AVX512 and AMX support for x86 architectures

stages.name: CUDA kernels
stages.summary: The compatible CUDA route uses NVIDIA GPU acceleration through llama.cpp’s configured GPU backend.

evidence.quote: This provides GPU acceleration using an NVIDIA GPU.

stages.name: MLX Metal kernels
stages.summary: MLX primitives for the illustrated Apple-silicon GPU work use Metal kernels.

evidence.quote: Apple silicon devices address their GPUs using the Metal shading language, and GPU kernels in MLX are written using Metal.

stages.name: CPU
stages.summary: The CPU-only example keeps the selected model in system memory and executes its numerical work on CPU.

evidence.quote: 100% CPU means the model was loaded entirely in system memory

stages.name: NVIDIA GPU
stages.summary: The CUDA example executes supported offloaded work on a compatible NVIDIA GPU; partial CPU offload is not shown.

evidence.quote: This provides GPU acceleration using an NVIDIA GPU.

stages.name: Apple silicon GPU
stages.summary: The supported MLX route executes its GPU primitives through Metal on Apple silicon.

evidence.quote: Apple silicon devices address their GPUs using the Metal shading language, and GPU kernels in MLX are written using Metal.
